findings.passage: Prosecutors then charged Lee over an email offered as evidence.
findings.problem: The paragraph never says what the email was, so the reader cannot see how the conviction bears on the allegation against Ellison. The opened source (Kalat, S11) says it was a note purporting to come from Lee's supervisor, Craig Ramsey, to Ellison, reading "Larry, I've terminated Adelyn per your request", which was the document tying the firing to Ellison. The prosecution's case was that Ramsey's car-phone records showed he was driving when it was sent and that its headers pointed to an address near Lee's home. Kalat and Ellison (S03) both say her account of what happened changed during the suit. With that left out, the closing caveat that the accounts come 'mostly from Oracle's side' leaves the retaliation claim reading as untested. Fairness runs the other way too: Kalat, citing the unopened Softwar, has Ellison writing that he 'decided not to veto' the supervisor's decision, which qualifies his quoted 'I never caused her to be fired'.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph states, attributed to Kalat, what the email purported to show and the basis of the prosecution's case, before Rockhill's counter-argument. The conviction, Ellison's denial and the sentence about what the conviction did not decide all remain. If 'I never caused her to be fired' stays, the 'decided not to veto' line is either included as secondhand from Softwar or left for the research task. No adjective is applied to Lee.

findings.passage: A Delaware court had already ruled in Ellison's favor over the same trades.
findings.problem: The plaintiffs' lawyer gets three sentences with share prices; the court finding gets one vague clause, and Ellison's own position is absent. A search for the ruling returned the Delaware Court of Chancery opinion of November 24, 2004 (In re Oracle Corp. Derivative Litigation, Vice Chancellor Strine), which granted summary judgment to Ellison and Jeffrey Henley and concluded that no rational trier of fact could find that either held material nonpublic information when he traded or acted with scienter. I read the search summary of the Justia copy, not the full opinion, and it is not among the run's sources. The standard asks for the evidence label ('court finding') and the person's response. 'Neither report records an admission' describes an absence in two wire stories that quote only the plaintiffs' lawyer (S12, S13).
findings.acceptance_test: The 2004 opinion (law.justia.com/cases/delaware/court-of-chancery/2004/54350-1.html) is opened and added as a source, and its finding is stated in one plain dated sentence. Ellison's or his counsel's stated position on the trades is quoted from an opened source, or the text says none was found in the opened record. Tabacco's argument and the settlement terms stay.

findings.passage: The report records no response from him.
findings.problem: True of the Bloomberg report (S18), but it reads as though he never answered, and he did. Search results for a Forbes interview published in April 2020 (reported by Business Insider and The Register on 2020-04-14) quote him: "I don't think he's the devil — I support him and want him to do well." The same coverage says he told Forbes he let Trump use the property and did not attend. I confirmed this through search results, not by opening Forbes. The evidence record already notes he was reportedly not present (C31 alternative), yet the draft's 'held at his Rancho Mirage estate' and 'his public support for Trump' leave the reader assuming he hosted in person.
findings.acceptance_test: The Forbes interview, or The Register's 2020-04-14 report of it, is opened and added as a source. His response is quoted with its date, and the text says he said he did not attend. The sentence 'The report records no response from him' is removed or limited to what Bloomberg recorded on February 20, 2020.

findings.passage: Oracle did not respond to the Post.
findings.problem: This sentence is not in the opened source. The Engadget summary (S17), re-fetched for this review, contains no statement about Oracle or Ellison being asked for comment, and the Washington Post article is unopened (C80's own review trigger). The same Engadget report does say 'He has seemingly never expressed doubts about the 2020 election results publicly', which is the only context in the opened record bearing on his position, and the draft leaves it out.
findings.acceptance_test: The Post article is opened and the non-response is attributed exactly (who was asked, who did not answer), or the sentence is removed. The paragraph adds, with attribution, that no public statement from him doubting the 2020 result was on record as of that report. 'It records nothing he said' stays.

findings.passage: "Citizens will be on their best behavior because we are constantly recording and reporting everything that's going on."
findings.problem: Two surveillance quotations are cut loose from the reasoning he gave with them. In the Business Insider report (S19) the sentence follows directly from: "We're going to have supervision. Every police officer is going to be supervised at all times, and if there's a problem, AI will report that problem and report it to the appropriate person." He began with watching the police; the draft presents only the state watching citizens. In the 2002 Playboy answer (S03), the 'blind luck' line follows "Can such intelligence be abused? Absolutely. Everything can be," and his argument that the government has 'a damn good record of using information'. That is his reply to the civil-liberties objection, and the section says only that the type reading 'does not answer' it. The framing also outruns three dated statements: 'has spent more than two decades arguing that the state should watch more' and 'something he has always liked'.
findings.acceptance_test: The 2024 quotation includes or accurately paraphrases the police-supervision sentences. The 2002 passage includes his acknowledgement that the information can be abused and the reason he gave for trusting the government. The framing sentences claim no more than three statements in 2002, 2013 and 2024. McAllister's commercial objection stays.

findings.passage: It cites resident Solomon Pili Kaho'ohalahala telling Bloomberg that Ellison had done little to control the invasive deer or protect the reefs
findings.problem: A specific charge of neglect reaches the page third-hand: an advocacy feature (S24) citing Bloomberg citing a resident. No response from Ellison or Pulama Lanai is given, and the re-fetched Nation piece records none. The draft then tells the reader its own sourcing is inadequate ('Residents on both sides deserve a fuller hearing than one advocacy piece provides'). The standard asks for a named critic's actual argument and the person's response, and C81's trigger says to replace the secondhand citation before publishing. 'It reads as the largest version of an environment he can completely control' also moves his phrase about a workplace onto an inhabited island as the author's inference.
findings.acceptance_test: The Bloomberg original is opened and the resident is cited firsthand with a date, with Pulama Lanai's or Ellison's response or a statement that the opened report records none. Otherwise the paragraph is cut to what the opened record supports: the purchase, the stated plan, and The Nation's argument labelled as argument. The sentence apologising for the sourcing is gone because the sourcing is fixed.

findings.passage: The record of what he does when he has to choose suggests he still gives the first answer.
findings.problem: The closing turns a finding about public conduct (control over approval) into a claim about what he privately puts ahead of love. The profile examined business and public choices only; it says itself that no former wife's or family member's account is part of it. The 2002 telling the piece opens and closes on continues, in the opened source (S03): "Of course she's right. We've got to find that someplace in our lives. It's why my extended family is very important. And my relationship with my children is especially important to me." His own stated resolution of the story is omitted, and the ending asserts the opposite. It also blurs the thesis: the argument is that he does not choose admiration, and the last line says he still chooses 'standing'.
findings.acceptance_test: The ending limits its claim to the observed public choices between approval and control. His own conclusion from the 2002 telling is quoted or paraphrased with attribution. No sentence states or implies what he privately prefers to love.

findings.passage: He agreed to give $100 million to charity in Oracle's name
findings.problem: This court settlement is the only mention of giving in a 3,700-word profile that covers seven controversies. The public record includes the 2010 Giving Pledge commitment (S34), a $200 million gift to USC noted in the evidence record's context for S05, the USC speech's 'give nearly all of it away' (S05), and his answer in the opened Playboy interview that he would spend 'All of it' to beat cancer: "Be the richest person on earth or be the guy who cured cancer?" (S03). The draft omits all of it because the philanthropy sources were not opened (research task). The effect is a page that lists what the pattern cost others and nothing he has given, which sits badly with the standard's 'neither defender nor prosecutor'. It is also type evidence either way.
findings.acceptance_test: One sourced, dated paragraph on his giving, built from opened primary material (the Giving Pledge letter, S03, S05), with no vouching for motive and any criticism of how he gives attributed to a named source. Failing that, the editor records why the opened record cannot support even that paragraph.

findings.passage: ## Caught with Microsoft's trash, he called a press conference
findings.problem: The heading says he was caught with Microsoft's trash. The body and The Register (S08) say a detective firm hired by Oracle 'was caught trying to buy' the office rubbish of a Microsoft-funded trade group. Ellison's 2002 account does speak of investigators 'going through Microsoft's garbage', so the target is his word against the news report, but 'he' was not the one caught and he says he did not know the method in advance. Two summary lines repeat the slippage: 'going through a rival's garbage' stated as fact, and 'he conceded nothing' two paragraphs after 'he conceded the unsavory part himself'.
findings.acceptance_test: The heading and summary sentences match the body's record of who did what to whose trash. His statement that he did not know the method beforehand sits next to the first description of the episode. 'Conceded nothing' is reconciled with 'Unsavory, yucky—kind of. But legal.'

findings.problem: Sayonara took line honours (first boat to finish). The race's overall winner on handicap in 1998 was AFR Midnight Rambler, per the race's published results as returned by search. The FAQ repeats 'His yacht Sayonara won the December 1998 race'. The FAQ also says he 'had not listened carefully enough to the warnings' and calls it 'his decision to race'. In the CNN transcript (S10) he says 'I guess we didn't listen carefully enough' and 'we go into these races', speaking of the sailors as a group after the narrator describes the fleet's choice. The rewrite turns a collective remark into a personal admission in a passage about six deaths.
findings.acceptance_test: Body and FAQ say Sayonara was first across the line or took line honours. Body and FAQ keep his 'we' and do not describe the remark as an admission about his own decision.

findings.passage: On CBS he recalled being told he would "never amount to anything,"
findings.problem: The same CBS passage (S04) carries Ellison's own account of why his father said it: "I think, because I was constantly questioning authority, that he felt that would continuously get me in trouble as it had in school -- as it had in the Boy Scouts, as it had on athletic teams." It is the only explanation of Louis Ellison's motive in the record, it is more charitable than the bare quotation, and the draft leaves it out while noting that the father cannot answer.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph includes Ellison's explanation of his father's remark, attributed as his own guess. The caveat that Louis Ellison's side is not on the record remains.

findings.passage: a public doubt about his word, answered with force and no explanation
findings.problem: Per Fortune (S20) the Warner Bros. Discovery board questioned the financing because it was tied to a revocable family trust; it did not doubt his word, and the announcement was the company's. The same report frames the guarantee as a father backing his son, a reading the draft does not offer while equating a financing term with the trash episode. Earlier in the section, 'quick, large, unhedged backing' outruns the opened report (S16): Musk proposed $2 billion 'or more' and Ellison settled on $1 billion. The research task says the exact texts should come from the court exhibit.
findings.acceptance_test: The guarantee is described as answering a doubt about the financing, with the father-and-son reading named beside the author's. 'Unhedged' is dropped or supported by the exhibit text, and the $2 billion recommendation is stated.

protected_passages.passage: That is one side of a relationship, told as a joke decades later. Louis Ellison's side is not on the record, so it stays a story Ellison tells and not a proven cause.
protected_passages.reason: Keeps a dead man's side open and refuses to turn a joke into a childhood wound. This is the standard's rule applied in the prose, where the reader can see it.

protected_passages.passage: A six-year-old afraid his mother will not come home fits every type equally. It is better left unexplained.
protected_passages.reason: Declines to convert his one admitted deep fear into type evidence or a causal theory.

protected_passages.passage: Each episode has a second reading. Milken was a wealthy, well-connected ally. Hiring Hurd was a coup against a competitor. A man with an outlaw's reputation can gain from owning a scandal loudly. Any one of these could be calculation.
protected_passages.reason: States the self-interested reading of each thesis-bearing act before drawing the inference, so the reader can tell record from interpretation.

protected_passages.passage: An Eight's need for control explains how a workplace, a marriage or a stock sale ends up arranged around one man's judgment. It is an explanation of the pattern and no defense of any instance of it.
protected_passages.reason: Explains without excusing and without a verdict line, as the controversy rules require.
Marks the exact limit of the evidence for the November 2020 call. Removing it would let a third party's email stand as proof of his position.

assessment: Fairness proxy only; I do not speak for Ellison. The draft is not a hit piece. It separates self-report from inference more carefully than most, admits the two unread biographies, gives the Type 3 case real room, and attaches a denial to the Lee, Paramount and trash episodes. The weakness is consistent: where his own answer or the exculpatory record exists, the page often stops short of it. The forged email is never described (subject-01), the Delaware finding is one clause (subject-02), his 2020 response on Trump is treated as nonexistent (subject-03), two surveillance quotes lose the reasoning he gave with them (subject-05), a Lanai charge arrives third-hand with no reply (subject-06), and the ending asserts a private preference that the opened source has him contradicting (subject-07). One sentence about a non-response is not in any opened source (subject-04). Seven controversies appear and no giving (subject-08). What I checked: I re-fetched 16 of the run's sources (S02, S03, S04, S07, S08, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S24) and read the sensitive passages in context; the quotations I checked are verbatim. Three points come from web search summaries, not opened pages: the Forbes 2020 response, the 2004 Delaware opinion and the 1998 race result. The editor should open them before acting. I did not re-open the 2025-2026 sources (S20-S23, S25), so the guarantee, the closing and the Robbins suit are unverified by me. 'The fighter jet' in the opening has no claim or source in the evidence record. Similarity advisory was available and did not trip (maximum 0.024 against a 0.04 threshold); the matches are incidental phrases, and the argument (two tellings of the sister story, control against approval) is specific to this subject. Risks: sensitive allegations (Lee, insider trading, the November 2020 call, the Robbins complaint) and contested typing (8 against 3 at medium confidence) both stand; the full jury is warranted.
